result.summary: After Numa's death his wife Egeria mourns in the grove at Aricia. Hippolytus, now Virbius, tries to comfort her with the story of his own death and revival, but she dissolves into a fountain. The Nymphs' wonder is compared to other marvels: Tages rising from a clod, Romulus' lance becoming a tree, and Cippus growing horns and choosing exile over kingship.

scenes.title: Numa's reign and Egeria's grief
scenes.summary: Numa returns, becomes king and brings peace to Rome. After his death Egeria flees to the Aricia valley and weeps there.
scenes.stakes: Egeria stands to lose herself in grief for her dead husband.

scenes.title: Hippolytus offers comfort
scenes.summary: The Nymphs and Hippolytus urge Egeria to stop weeping and consider the sorrows of others.

scenes.title: Hippolytus' death
scenes.summary: Falsely accused by his step-mother and cursed by Theseus, Hippolytus is driven away. A sea-bull frightens his horses and he is dragged to a mangled death.
scenes.stakes: Hippolytus' life, destroyed by false accusation and a father's curse.

scenes.title: Revival as Virbius
scenes.summary: Healed by the son of Apollo against Pluto's will, Hippolytus is hidden by Cynthia and renamed Virbius in her grove.

scenes.title: Egeria becomes a fountain
scenes.summary: Egeria dissolves in tears and Diana turns her into a spring, astonishing the Nymphs and Virbius.
scenes.stakes: Egeria's grief dissolves her into water.

scenes.title: Tages and Romulus' lance
scenes.summary: Comparisons: an Etrurian clod becomes the prophet Tages, and Romulus' lance becomes a tree.

scenes.title: Cippus's horns and refusal
scenes.summary: Cippus sees horns on his head, is told by the soothsayer that he will be king, and refuses. He warns the Romans to expel him.
scenes.stakes: Cippus risks his country's liberty and gives up a crown for exile.

scenes.title: The people honour Cippus
scenes.summary: The crowd searches for the horns. Cippus reveals them, and the Romans crown him, grant him land and carve his horns on the gates.

alias_notes.explanation: Name given to Hippolytus by Diana after his revival.
Epithet of Diana, from Mount Cynthus on Delos.

notable_quotes.reason: Cippus prefers exile to becoming king, a classic Roman statement of anti-monarchical virtue.

analysis.text: Metamorphosis is tied to grief, consolation and change of identity: Egeria dissolves, Hippolytus is renamed. Cippus shows the Roman ideal of civic duty over ambition.
The Cippus tale reflects Roman horror of kingship and reverence for the Republic's liberty, a theme that would speak to readers in Augustus' time.

legacy.text: Egeria's name came to mean a woman adviser or inspirer, and her spring at Nemi was a real cult site.

fun_facts.text: Diana's grove at Nemi, where Virbius was worshipped, is the setting of Frazer's The Golden Bough (1890).

language_notes.text: "Cultivated" is used figuratively: Numa's mind is tilled like a field with teachings, here the philosophical precepts he learned from Pythagoras at Croton.
"Inured" means accustomed or hardened by long experience.
"Latian" means Latin, belonging to Latium, the region around Rome.
Orestes was said to have brought Diana's cult image from Tauris to Italy, where it was worshipped at Aricia.
The "son of Theseus" is Hippolytus, who died when his horses bolted, and was restored to life by Diana, living in Aricia as Virbius.
Pasiphaë's daughter is Phaedra, Theseus' wife and Hippolytus' step-mother; she is identified only by her mother, who was known for her unnatural passion for a bull.
Imprecations are curses; Theseus asks his father Neptune to destroy his son.
Phlegethon is the river of fire in the underworld, so bathing in it means he actually died and entered the realm of the dead.
Pæonian aid means healing; Pæon was the physician of the gods. The son of Apollo is Aesculapius, god of medicine, who revived Hippolytus.
Virbius is generally explained as 'twice a man' (vir bis), a name marking his second life.
The sister of Phœbus is Diana. Egeria, a nymph, mourned the death of her husband, King Numa, just before this scene.
The son of the Amazon is Hippolytus, restored to life and now called Virbius, who lived in Diana's grove at Aricia.
Etrurian means from Etruria, the region of central Italy later called Tuscany, famed for its divination.
Romulus' lance: the legend says his spear, thrown onto the Palatine hill, took root and grew into a cornel tree.
Quirinus is the name given to the deified Romulus; 'people of Quirinus' means the Romans.
Consulting 'panting entrails' refers to haruspicy, divination by reading the organs of sacrificed animals, still quivering.
Latian means of Latium, the region around Rome.
Laurel was a symbol of peace and victory, so it serves here as a cover for the horns.
An augur was a priest who foretold events from signs; here he is the same Etrurian soothsayer.
The grant is as much land as oxen could plough around in a day, from sunrise to sunset.

context_notes.text: Virbius was a minor Italian god associated with Diana's grove at Aricia, identified with Hippolytus.
Numa Pompilius, Rome's second king, was traditionally the founder of its religious institutions. His wife was the nymph Egeria, who advised him.
Aricia, near Rome, had a famous grove and temple of Diana, goddess of the hunt and of woodland.
Trœzen was the city of Pittheus, Theseus' maternal grandfather, where Hippolytus had been raised.
Cynthia is Diana, a title from Mount Cynthus on Delos. Hippolytus was her devoted follower, so she shelters him.
Tages was the Etruscan founder of divination, said to have taught the Etruscans the rules of reading entrails.
Rome hated the idea of kings after expelling Tarquin, which explains Cippus's horror at being called king.

literary_notes.text: The narrator's exclamation "Ah!" expresses sympathy and draws the reader into Egeria's sorrow.
The repeated "Ah! how oft... Ah! how often" stresses the long persistence of her grief and the efforts to console her.
Hippolytus wishes for a comforting example not his own, yet admits his own fate, a violent death, can console her.
The sea monster is described as a bull rising like a living beast, making the water seem a menacing agent of fate.
Hippolytus stays fearless, absorbed in his unjust exile, while the attendants and horses panic, a calm that soon proves useless.
The long, graphic list of bodily damage, with its noises and torn limbs, makes the horror vivid, ending in the stark summary of one wound.
Hippolytus challenges the nymph Egeria to say her grief matches his, framing his tale as consolation by comparison.
Virbius's astonishment is compared to that of the Etrurian ploughman at the clod turning into Tages, linking transformation stories.
Cippus addresses the gods directly, and his prayer puts his country's welfare before his own.
The crowd's noise is compared to wind in pines and distant waves, making the din vivid and natural.
The parenthetical aside stresses the surprising reversal: the people who dread a king now look on his horns with respect.
